interviewQuestions.question: How would you structure CSS for a 200-component design system used by multiple teams?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the failure mode this has to prevent: at 200 components across multiple teams, plain global CSS guarantees collisions, and convention alone (BEM) relies on every contributor following the rule perfectly forever, which doesn't survive scale or team turnover.

So I'd want a **structural** isolation guarantee, not a convention — either CSS Modules (unique generated class names per file, works with plain CSS syntax) or a utility-first system (shared low-specificity atoms with nothing custom to collide). Between those two, the deciding factor is usually whether the team is willing to write markup utility-class-heavy in exchange for enforced visual consistency — a design system's whole point is consistency, so utility-first's constraint is often a feature, not a bug, for exactly this use case.

Whatever the base choice, I'd wrap the system in an explicit `@layer` order — say `reset, tokens, components, overrides` — so consuming teams have a guaranteed, predictable place to slot their own overrides without needing `!important` or fighting the design system's internal specificity. That combination — structural scoping plus explicit layer ordering — is what actually holds up as the system grows past what any one person can review by eye.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about isolation and override-ability together, not just pick a framework by name.

interviewQuestions.question: What's the real trade-off between CSS Modules and CSS-in-JS, beyond "one uses files and one uses JS"?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The surface difference is syntax, but the real trade-off is **when scoping happens and what capability that buys you**. CSS Modules resolve scoping entirely at build time — the bundler rewrites class names before anything ships, so there's no runtime cost at all, but the styles are static: you can't compute a color from a live prop value without falling back to inline styles or conditional class toggling.

Classic CSS-in-JS resolves scoping (and the styles themselves) partly or fully at runtime, which is what lets you write `background: ${props => props.theme.primary}` directly inline — genuinely dynamic styling with no separate class-toggling dance. The cost is real: computing and injecting styles in the browser on every render is measurably slower than parsing a static stylesheet once, and it shows up in profiling on style-heavy pages.

In practice I'd reach for CSS Modules when styling is mostly static with a handful of toggled states (a `.card.featured` variant is fine as a conditional class), and CSS-in-JS when a component's styling is genuinely a function of continuously varying data — a chart component coloring bars by a computed value, for instance. Compile-time CSS-in-JS variants exist specifically to claw back the runtime cost while keeping most of the dynamic ergonomics, which is worth mentioning if the team already leans CSS-in-JS but is runtime-cost-sensitive.

**Testing:** whether you understand the underlying cost model, not just that one syntax looks more "modern."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: How would you migrate a large app's global CSS to CSS Modules without stopping feature work for weeks?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't attempt a big-bang rewrite — freezing feature delivery to convert every stylesheet at once is a hard sell to any business, and a half-finished big-bang migration is a worse state than the original problem, because now two systems exist and neither is fully trustworthy.

The approach I'd actually run: every *new* component is written in CSS Modules from day one — zero cost, since it's greenfield. Existing components stay on the old global CSS until they're touched for an unrelated reason — a bug fix, a redesign — at which point converting them rides along with work that was happening anyway. Both systems coexist safely during the transition specifically because CSS Modules' whole design goal is not colliding with anything else on the page.

The one real risk during coexistence I'd explicitly check for: an unconverted file might reach into a component that's already been converted, using the old global class name in its own selector — `.old-card .icon { }` targeting a component whose markup no longer has `.old-card` at all. That fails silently rather than loudly, so before deleting any old class name I'd grep the whole codebase for references to it first.

**Testing:** whether you can plan an incremental migration with a real safety check, rather than proposing an unrealistic rewrite.

interviewQuestions.question: A junior engineer asks why the team doesn't just use plain CSS everywhere since it's simpler. How do you answer that without dismissing the question?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's a genuinely reasonable question, and the honest answer is that plain CSS is simpler right up until the codebase has enough components and enough contributors that the single global namespace stops being safe to reason about by eye. On a five-page site with one contributor, plain CSS is the correct choice — none of BEM, CSS Modules, CSS-in-JS, or utility-first earn their overhead there.

The concrete failure mode I'd walk them through: two teams, each writing a `.card` class independently, both loaded on the same page. Neither did anything wrong in isolation — CSS just has no built-in concept of "this class belongs to this component only," so whichever stylesheet happens to load later silently overrides the other's padding. At a handful of components that's a five-minute bug to find; at hundreds of components across multiple teams, it becomes a recurring, hard-to-attribute source of "I touched an unrelated feature and something on another page broke."

Every scoping approach — naming convention, build-time renaming, runtime generation, shared utility atoms — exists purely to give CSS the module boundary it never had, once the project has grown past the point where a person can hold every existing class name in their head.

**Testing:** whether you can explain a technical trade-off to someone earlier-career without being condescending, and whether you actually understand why the complexity exists rather than just following it as convention.
